lecture_context.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models

unit.name: Data poisoning, backdoors, and prompt injection
unit.description: Covers attacks that enter through training data or natural-language instructions, including trigger-based image backdoors and direct or indirect prompt injection.
unit.summary: Backdoor attacks are introduced as increasingly common because large models often train on scraped data, giving attackers a chance to plant triggers before deployment [ts=2344s]. In the cat/dog example, a small patch is inserted and mislabeled so that the trained model later treats the trigger as evidence for the attacker’s target class [ts=2370s]. The same pattern can generalize beyond images when scraped text contains malicious associations that may later activate a deployment-time behavior [ts=2468s]. Prompt injection is then defined through an LLM application where user input is concatenated with a prompt template and malicious text like “ignore previous instructions” changes the effective instruction seen by the model [ts=2694s]. The instructor distinguishes direct prompt injection from indirect attacks hidden in retrieved webpages or tool outputs, which can affect agents using search or retrieval [ts=2805s].

key_points.text: Backdoor attacks can be introduced when scraped or shared training data contains attacker-controlled triggers.
A trigger patch plus intentional mislabeling can teach the model to associate the trigger with the attacker’s target label.
Red teaming, RLHF, constitutional AI, safety nets, input sanitization, and data review are discussed as imperfect backdoor defenses.
Prompt injection can override an LLM application’s intended prompt by mixing malicious user text into the combined prompt.
Indirect prompt injection can arrive from a secondary source, such as a retrieved website read by an agent.

kp_catalog.name: Backdoor and data poisoning attacks
kp_catalog.description: Training-data attacks where hidden triggers or malicious data patterns cause targeted deployment-time behavior after the model has been trained.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The cat/dog trigger example makes the mechanism concrete: insert trigger, train, deploy, then activate the trigger [ts=2370s][ts=2430s].

kp_catalog.name: Prompt injection
kp_catalog.description: Attack on LLM applications where malicious text alters the effective instruction seen by the model, either directly from user input or indirectly from retrieved context.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The lecture defines prompt injection through a combined prompt template and later distinguishes direct from indirect attacks [ts=2694s][ts=2805s].

kp_catalog.name: Adversarial defense strategies
kp_catalog.description: Defenses including safety nets, input sanitization, output filtering, adversarial training, red teaming, RLHF, and constitutional AI, none of which fully eliminates the attack-defense arms race.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The instructor surveys defenses and stresses that attacks and defenses evolve together [ts=2041s][ts=2226s].
